<explanation>
The Gem Wallet project is a robust, full-featured iOS wallet application built in SwiftUI that leverages a modular architecture. It is organized into multiple independent feature modules (located under the “Features” directory), various service layers (under “Services”), and a suite of packages that provide blockchain integration, cryptography (via a Rust core library), UI components, and utilities. Below is an explanation of how to capture all these essential layers and components in a comprehensive system design diagram.

1. Project Overview and Main Components
   • Application Frontend (UI)
     – Built using SwiftUI and organized into numerous feature modules (e.g., Onboarding, WalletTab, Swap, Staking, PriceAlerts, NFT, QRScanner, etc.).
     – Each module often follows an MVVM pattern: Scenes (views), ViewModels, and supporting types.
   • Navigation and App Coordination
     – Look at the Gem/Core folder and Gem/Root navigation and view models. These are the central coordinators that manage the app’s navigation and scene switching.
   • Service Layer
     – The “Services” directory provides backend support for business logic such as asset management, balance updates, notifications, blockchain data retrieval, node status, transaction processing, and WalletConnect.
   • Data and Domain Libraries
     – Packages such as Blockchain, Keystore, Primitives, and WalletCore supply critical infrastructure (e.g., secure cryptographic operations, multi-chain support, and key management).
     – The “Store” package handles persistence (database, migrations, models for balances, transactions, etc.).
   • UI Components & Styling
     – Packages/Components and Packages/Style present reusable UI elements like list views, buttons, and custom controls, which ensure consistency across the application.
   • External Integrations and Third-Party Communication
     – GemAPI handles network requests toward external endpoints.
     – SwiftHTTPClient abstracts HTTP communication.
     – Integration with a Rust-based “Core” library provides secure cryptographic operations.
   
2. Layered Architecture and Relationships
   • Presentation Layer:
     – Depict multiple feature modules (each with Scenes and ViewModels) as a cluster. Connect these to a central “App Coordinator/Navigation” component which orchestrates scene transitions.
   • Business Logic / Service Layer:
     – Represent services (e.g., AssetsService, BalanceService, PriceService, ChainService, etc.) as a separate block that the view models call into.
     – Show directional arrows from the Presentation Layer (via view models) to each relevant service component.
   • Data & Domain Layer:
     – Diagram the domain libraries (Blockchain, Keystore, Primitives, etc.) that are consumed by the service layer.
     – Connect the Service Layer to the Data Layer via arrows that represent data retrieval, cryptographic validation, and key management.
   • External and Infrastructure Layer:
     – External dependencies such as GemAPI and SwiftHTTPClient should be shown, along with the communication with external blockchain networks and dApps (used with WalletConnect).
     – Include the “Core” Rust library (found under the core submodule and referenced in Gem’s README) as a secure cryptographic engine.
   • Persistence:
     – The “Store” package is responsible for local database interactions. It should be depicted as a storage block that feeds data into the Service Layer.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles
   • MVVM Pattern is prominently used within each feature module:
     – Each module has clear separation between its Scene (View) and ViewModel; annotate this in the diagram.
   • Modularization using Swift Packages:
     – Use separate boxes for each package (Blockchain, Keystore, Localization, etc.), noting that each module is integrated via a Package.swift manifest.
   • Dependency Inversion & Abstraction:
     – Service interfaces (protocols) and use of dependency injection (seen under Gem/Core/AppResolver) to allow for testability and replaceable implementations.
   • Separation of Concerns:
     – Clearly show the boundary between UI (presentation), business logic (services), and low-level domain operations (data/crypto packages).

4. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines
   For a full-stack mobile wallet application like Gem Wallet, the diagram should emphasize:
   • A distinct separation between the UI (frontend feature modules grouped by functionality), and the backend “service” or “domain” layers.
   • A clear arrowed flow:
       – From user action on SwiftUI views → view models → various services → domain libraries/Blockchain modules → persistence layer.
   • Integration Points:
       – Highlight WalletConnect’s service interconnecting with external dApps.
       – Note the role of the Rust “Core” library in delivering cryptographic functions.
       – Display modular interdependencies between various Packages (e.g., Keystore for authentication, Primitives for asset and chain management).
   • Technologies and Frameworks:
       – SwiftUI (for the frontend), Swift Package Manager (integrating many packages), and Rust for the core secure functionalities.

5. Practical Guidelines for the Diagram
   • Use clear labels for each component. For example, label boxes as “Onboarding Module,” “WalletTab Module,” “BalanceService,” “Blockchain Package,” etc.
   • Display directional arrows to indicate data flow or dependencies:
       – From UI components to view models;
       – From view models to service interfaces;
       – From services to lower-level packages and external interfaces.
   • Use color coding or shapes to distinguish types: you might choose a specific color for UI layers (e.g., blue), another for services (e.g., green), and another for infrastructure/domain packages (e.g., orange).
   • Ensure every module in the file tree is captured in your abstraction, mapping the key areas rather than every individual file, so that the diagram remains both comprehensive and legible.
   • Group related features and packages into subsystem clusters (e.g., “Features,” “Services,” “Packages/Domain,” “UI Components/Style”).

6. Final Check
   • Verify that the diagram reflects the high-level flow: UI (user interaction, navigation) → Business Logic (service calls, Wallet management, Network requests via GemAPI/HTTP Client) → Domain (Blockchain integration, Cryptographic operations using Core/Rust, Local data persistence via Store).
   • Illustrate connectors between modules for features like WalletConnect which bridges to external dApps.
   • Make sure naming conventions align with the project (e.g., “Gem Wallet,” “AssetsService,” “ChainService”) and that visual elements (shapes, colors) clearly distinguish between UI components, service layers, and infrastructure libraries.

This detailed explanation should give you a clear guideline on constructing a system design diagram that accurately reflects the layered, modular architecture of the Gem Wallet project. The goal is to capture its separation of concerns, the flow of data from the user interface through business logic to external services, and the integration of multiple domain-specific packages that together form a secure, responsive mobile wallet.
</explanation>
